power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps ≤ .003", Text = "Barrier-specific marginal contrasts showed that Chinese-heritage parents rated seven of the nine barriers as more relevant than White parents (all ps ≤ .003; Table 3); no significant group differences were found for \"not needing more parenting knowledge\" (p = .24) or data security concerns (p = .66)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. text.text: Objective: Preventive parenting programs can reduce child mental health risks, but equitable reach requires effective recruitment.
Little is known about how recruitment messaging can engage underserved culturally diverse families while retaining broad population appeal.
We compared responses to recruitment messaging and participation barriers among Chinese-heritage and White parents.
Methods: Parents of children aged 2-5 years (100 Chinese-heritage, 101 White) in Englishspeaking Western countries were recruited online.

Participants rated six parenting program recruitment messages based on the Theory of Planned Behaviour, Goal-Directed Behaviour, Norm Activation Model, their combination, or Chinese cultural values (guan and harmony), and nine participation barriers.
Mixed-effects regression models examined participation likelihood, perceived program usefulness, and barrier relevance by ethnicity and message/barrier type.
Results: Chinese-heritage parents reported lower participation likelihood and perceived program usefulness, and higher average barrier relevance than White parents.

Ethnicity-bymessage interactions were not significant; descriptively, guan was highest rated among Chinese-heritage parents and Goal-Directed Behaviour among White parents, while the combined behavioural theory message was highly rated across groups.
Ethnicity-by-barrier interactions were significant: Chinese-heritage parents rated seven of nine barriers as more relevant compared to White parents.
Lack of time was most relevant among Chineseheritage parents; concern about data security was most relevant among White parents, although its relevance did not differ significantly between groups.

Conclusions: Findings extend research on cultural adaptation to recruitment, and highlight the need to balance cultural responsiveness with broad appeal while addressing families' differing barriers to participation.

Evidence-based parenting programs have been shown to improve child development and prevent later mental health problems by addressing modifiable parental risk factors (Jeong et al., 2021; Yap et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Evidence-based parenting programs have been shown to improve child development and prevent later mental health problems by addressing modifiable parental risk factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Jeong et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Yap et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, their preventive potential depends not only on intervention effectiveness but also on whether families can access and participate in them.
Participation in population-based parenting programs remains low, particularly among underserved culturally diverse populations, such as Chinese-heritage families (Pote et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Participation in population-based parenting programs remains low, particularly among underserved culturally diverse populations, such as Chinese-heritage families <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Pote et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Unequal access may limit the population-level benefits of parenting programs and contribute to disparities in child mental health outcomes (Huang et al., 2012; Kouider et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Unequal access may limit the population-level benefits of parenting programs and contribute to disparities in child mental health outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Huang et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Kouider et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Improving recruitment may hence be an important component of equitable prevention.

Recruitment messaging may influence whether parents perceive a program as relevant and useful, and culturally tailored approaches have shown promise in engaging culturally diverse families (Huang & Shen, 2016).
text.formatted: Recruitment messaging may influence whether parents perceive a program as relevant and useful, and culturally tailored approaches have shown promise in engaging culturally diverse families <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Huang & Shen, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, developing separate approaches for every cultural group may not be feasible to implement at scale.
A key implementation challenge is to identify approaches that engage underserved groups while retaining broader population appeal (Sanders et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A key implementation challenge is to identify approaches that engage underserved groups while retaining broader population appeal <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Sanders et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, the Reach dimension and Equity focus of the RE-AIM implementation framework consider whether strategies reach underserved families and are effective across groups (Glasgow et al., 2019; Shelton et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Similarly, the Reach dimension and Equity focus of the RE-AIM implementation framework consider whether strategies reach underserved families and are effective across groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Glasgow et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Shelton et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, the present study compares broadly appealing messaging informed by behavioural change theories with culturally tailored messaging incorporating culturally salient values, examining messaging responses and perceived participation barriers among Chinese-heritage and White parents.

Behavioural change theories identify determinants that may influence participation across diverse populations, including attitudes, perceived behavioural control, social norms, and personal responsibility (Pope et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Behavioural change theories identify determinants that may influence participation across diverse populations, including attitudes, perceived behavioural control, social norms, and personal responsibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Pope et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Recruitment messages incorporating these Preprint: Submitted to Mental Health & Prevention, 9 Nov 2026 RECRUITING FAMILIES INTO PREVENTIVE PARENTING PROGRAMS 4 behavioural motivators may therefore improve participation in preventive programs across cultural groups, as previously demonstrated in public health settings (Pope et al., 2017).

text.text: This study examines three theories describing trait-based rather than threat-based behavioural determinants: the Theory of Planned Behaviour, Goal-Directed Behaviour, and the Norm Activation Model.

Together, they address attitudes, social norms, perceived behavioural control, emotional, motivational and habitual processes, and personal norms arising from awareness of benefits and responsibilities (Han, 2021; Perugini & Bagozzi, 2001).
text.formatted: Together, they address attitudes, social norms, perceived behavioural control, emotional, motivational and habitual processes, and personal norms arising from awareness of benefits and responsibilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Han, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Perugini & Bagozzi, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Although behavioural theory has informed research on parenting program engagement, studies have primarily examined individual theoretical constructs rather than directly evaluating theoryinformed recruitment messages, and have mostly involved White participants (Gonzalez et al., 2023; Thornton & Calam, 2011).
text.formatted: Although behavioural theory has informed research on parenting program engagement, studies have primarily examined individual theoretical constructs rather than directly evaluating theoryinformed recruitment messages, and have mostly involved White participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Gonzalez et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Thornton & Calam, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Whether such messages appeal similarly to culturally diverse parents, or how they compare to culturally tailored messaging, remains unclear.
An alternative approach is to culturally tailor recruitment messaging by incorporating culturally salient values.

While adapting surface-level elements such as language and visuals can increase familiarity and initial receptivity, deep-level tailoring that incorporates culturally meaningful values and beliefs may increase perceived relevance and more strongly influence behavioural intentions (Huang & Shen, 2016; Resnicow et al., 2000).
text.formatted: While adapting surface-level elements such as language and visuals can increase familiarity and initial receptivity, deep-level tailoring that incorporates culturally meaningful values and beliefs may increase perceived relevance and more strongly influence behavioural intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Huang & Shen, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Resnicow et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Culturally tailored parenting program recruitment messaging may increase perceived relevance by connecting program goals with culturally salient parenting values.
However, cultural groups are not homogeneous, and the relevance of particular values should be empirically evaluated rather than assumed (Pasick et al., 1996; Resnicow et al., 2000).

text.text: This study focuses on guan and harmony because both have established relevance in Chinese parenting research and can be connected to the goals of emotion-focused parenting programs (Chao, 1994; Pearson & Rao, 2003).
text.formatted: This study focuses on guan and harmony because both have established relevance in Chinese parenting research and can be connected to the goals of emotion-focused parenting programs <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Chao, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Pearson & Rao, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Although these values have informed research on parenting beliefs and practices, their potential relevance to parenting program recruitment has received little attention.

Comparing culturally tailored messages with behavioural theory-informed alternatives may help identify approaches relevant to Chinese-heritage parents without necessarily limiting their broader appeal.

A White comparison group, representing the majority in English-speaking Western countries, was included to provide an indication of whether messages that may appeal to Chinese-heritage parents also retain broader population appeal.
This is particularly relevant to population-based prevention, where recruitment strategies need to reach underserved families while remaining feasible for implementation across the wider population.
Importantly, the comparison is intended to examine group differences in recruitment responses, rather than to treat White parents as a normative benchmark for participation.
Alongside message relevance, understanding participation barriers is essential for improving the reach of preventive parenting programs (Glasgow et al., 2019; Sanders et al., 2026).

text.text: Parents commonly report logistical barriers, including time constraints, travel and childcare constraints, as well as psychological barriers such as stigma, fear of judgement, and concerns about program relevance (Koerting et al., 2013).

text.text: However, much of this evidence comes from predominantly White samples, including research on digitally delivered parenting programs (Breitenstein et al., 2014; Corralejo & Rodríguez, 2018; Westrupp et al., 2020).

text.text: Although digital delivery may reduce some logistical obstacles, it does not necessarily address psychological or cultural concerns.
Identifying the barriers that parents perceive as most relevant can therefore inform recruitment and delivery approaches that better accommodate diverse families.

Guided by the Reach dimension and Equity focus of RE-AIM (Glasgow et al., 2019; Shelton et al., 2020), this study examines recruitment messaging and perceived participation barriers as potentially modifiable components in the equitable implementation of preventive parenting programs.

(2) Test associations between recruitment message type and ratings of participation likelihood and perceived program usefulness among Chinese-heritage and White parents.

text.formatted: Margins Plot of Predicted Barrier Relevance Ratings by Barrier Type and Ethnicity Preprint: Submitted to Mental Health & Prevention, 9 Nov 2026 RECRUITING FAMILIES INTO PREVENTIVE PARENTING PROGRAMS 18 Discussion To our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically compare parenting program recruitment messages informed by three distinct behavioural change theories, examine culturally tailored messaging alongside behavioural theory-informed approaches, and investigate how both messaging responses and perceived participation barriers differ between Chinese-heritage and White parents.

text.text: By integrating these aims, this study extends cultural adaptation research beyond intervention content and delivery to examine recruitment as an important, yet underexamined, component of preventive intervention implementation.

Chinese-heritage parents reported lower participation likelihood and perceived program usefulness, alongside higher average perceived barrier relevance than White parents, although group differences varied across barriers.
Specifically, Chinese-heritage parents rated guanbased messaging most highly, whereas White parents preferred Goal-Directed Behaviour messaging.
Nonetheless, the Behavioural Mix message was favourably rated across both groups.
The most relevant participation barrier was lack of time for Chinese-heritage parents, and data security concerns for White parents.

Together, these findings offer new insight into how recruitment can balance cultural responsiveness and broader population appeal, while considering the different barriers that families may face in accessing preventive interventions.

Chinese-heritage parents' lower participation likelihood and perceived program usefulness, alongside greater perceived barriers, are consistent with evidence that culturally diverse families often face greater barriers to engaging with parenting interventions (Pote et al., 2019; Reid, 2001).

text.text: Previous research suggests Chinese-heritage parents may perceive parenting programs as culturally irrelevant, ineffective, difficult to apply, or too timeintensive (Ho et al., 2012; Lau et al., 2011; Wei et al., 2024).

text.text: Programs may additionally be perceived as less aligned with Chinese parents' emphasis on children's academic achievement and moral development (Chao, 1994; Ma, 2017).

text.text: These findings reinforce the importance of considering not only how preventive parenting programs are delivered, but also how their relevance and value are communicated to families who may be less likely to engage.

Guan-based messaging was the highest rated approach among Chinese-heritage parents. guan emphasises parental guidance, discipline, and support for children's learning (Chan et al., 2009; Chao, 1994; Guo, 2006; Wang et al., 2024), while also incorporating parental warmth and behavioural guidance, dimensions of authoritative parenting valued in Western contexts (Stewart et al., 2002).

text.text: Notably, guan was not associated with differences in participation likelihood or perceived usefulness ratings between Chinese-heritage and White parents.
This suggests that messaging reflecting culturally meaningful parenting values may resonate with the intended population without necessarily limiting broader appeal.
In contrast, harmony-based messaging was not among the highest rated approaches among Chinese-heritage parents.
Its emphasis on broad relational outcomes, rather than concrete parenting actions or child development goals, may have made it less relevant to parents' immediate priorities.
Harmony may also have been less salient for some of the firstgeneration immigrant families who may have had limited opportunities to navigate extendedfamily relationships post-migration.
More broadly, Chinese cultural values may be shifting towards a more mixed collectivistic-individualistic orientation (Li et al., 2006; Rao et al., 2001).
text.formatted: More broadly, Chinese cultural values may be shifting towards a more mixed collectivistic-individualistic orientation <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Li et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Rao et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: These explanations are speculative, but highlight that cultural tailoring is not inherently effective: values reflected in messages need to be meaningful to families, and relevant to their goals and circumstances.

White parents rated the Goal-Directed Behaviour message most highly, whereas Theory of Planned Behaviour messaging was lowest rated overall despite its prominence in behavioural research and previous associations with parenting program participation intentions (Gonzalez et al., 2023; Thornton & Calam, 2011).
text.formatted: White parents rated the Goal-Directed Behaviour message most highly, whereas Theory of Planned Behaviour messaging was lowest rated overall despite its prominence in behavioural research and previous associations with parenting program participation intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Gonzalez et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Thornton & Calam, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The Goal-Directed Behaviour message's emphasis on emotions, habits, and motivations may have resonated more strongly than the Theory of Planned Behaviour message's focus on attitudes, social norms, and behavioural control.
Notably, the Behavioural Mix message was highly rated by both groups.

Furthermore, although Chinese-heritage parents reported lower overall ratings, the ethnicityby-message interactions were not significant, indicating no clear evidence that group differences varied across message types.

From an implementation perspective, these findings suggest that integrating complementary behavioural motivators may offer a practical approach to recruitment messaging across diverse populations, without requiring separate messages for every cultural group.
However, the potential for broader reach requires testing with additional cultural groups and in real-world recruitment settings.
Chinese-heritage parents reported greater perceived barrier relevance than White parents overall and across seven of the nine barriers.
However, the magnitude of group differences varied by barrier type, indicating that specific barriers differed in salience between groups.
Lack of time was the most relevant barrier among Chinese-heritage parents.

This may reflect economic pressures associated with working long hours (Guo, 2006), alongside substantial investment in children's academic development and extra-curricular activities (Guo, 2014; Wang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This may reflect economic pressures associated with working long hours <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Guo, 2006)</ref>, alongside substantial investment in children's academic development and extra-curricular activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Guo, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Wang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Recruitment strategies targeting Chinese-heritage families may therefore benefit from emphasising flexibility, minimising time commitments, and communicating how participation can support child development and family wellbeing.
Data security concerns were the most relevant barrier among White parents, although perceived relevance did not differ significantly between groups.

Such concerns may reflect broader issues of confidentiality (Koerting et al., 2013), uncertainty about app-based services, or differences in trust in digital technologies across populations (Herbert et al., 2025; Kostka, 2023).

text.text: Notably, the high relevance rating of data security concerns and low rating of not needing more knowledge across both groups indicate that some barriers may be shared across populations.

While the reasons underlying these patterns require further investigation, these findings highlight the value of identifying families' specific concerns when implementing preventive parenting programs, including clearly communicating privacy and data security safeguards for digitally delivered interventions.
Several limitations should be considered.

First, participants were recruited through an online convenience sample, and their distribution across countries differed between the Chinese-heritage and White groups, with particularly limited representation of White parents in Australia and Canada.

Country was therefore not included as a covariate in the primary analyses, reflecting the study's focus on comparing overall responses across the Englishspeaking Western countries represented, rather than estimating within-country ethnic-group differences.

The multi-country sample nevertheless extends beyond a single national context, and other participant characteristics were broadly comparable with previous studies of digitally delivered parenting programs in Western countries (Breitenstein et al., 2021; Havighurst et al., 2024).

text.text: However, the uneven country distribution means that observed group differences may partly reflect variation in the national contexts represented.
Future research with larger and more balanced samples across countries could examine whether these associations are consistent across national contexts.

text.text: Findings may therefore not generalise to Chinese-heritage parents with limited English proficiency, although they remain relevant to many interventions delivered in English-speaking Western countries.
Third, outcomes reflected hypothetical participation intentions and perceived usefulness rather than actual enrolment or engagement.
Future research should test whether culturally tailored and broader theory-informed recruitment strategies translate into greater real-world program enrolment and sustained engagement.
Research should also investigate whether addressing practical and contextual barriers, such as time constraints and data security concerns, improves engagement across different families.

Conclusion By comparing recruitment messages grounded in different behavioural change theories and culturally tailored approaches, this study provides an initial examination of how alternative recruitment strategies may appeal to Chinese-heritage and White parents.

It also extends understanding of equitable access to preventive interventions by identifying both greater overall perceived barriers among Chinese-heritage parents and differences in specific barriers reported across groups.

Guan-based messaging was highest rated among Chineseheritage parents without being less favourably rated by White parents, while the Behavioural Mix message showed relatively broad appeal across both groups.
Participation barriers also varied, with lack of time most relevant among Chinese-heritage parents, and data security concerns most relevant among White parents.

These findings highlight recruitment as an important consideration in the implementation of preventive parenting programs, suggesting that strategies should balance cultural responsiveness with broader population appeal while addressing families' practical and contextual barriers.
Evaluating these approaches in realworld settings will be an important next step towards more equitable and effective ways of recruiting families into preventive parenting programs.
